tldr: This study makes the Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbone depth, action expert depth, and denoising steps independently configurable, allocating compute budgets based on the task to cut latency by roughly 80% while actually boosting the success rate.
hero_caption: Configuration of three compute axes in a flow-matching VLA (VLM depth V, action expert depth A, and denoising steps D), along with Pareto frontiers on Meta-World tasks. Jointly tuning these three axes drastically reduces latency and FLOPs compared to the full-compute base model while improving task success rates.
overview:
In robot control, flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models—which pair a large Vision-Language Model (VLM) with a flow-matching action expert that generates continuous robot trajectories—have gained tremendous momentum. However, their massive parameter counts and the need to run iterative denoising loops for every generated action lead to high inference latency, posing a major bottleneck for real-time hardware control.

Existing acceleration approaches typically truncate the layers of the VLM backbone (early exits), which accounts for most parameters, or decrease the number of denoising steps. Meanwhile, the depth of the action expert—which runs inside every denoising step and heavily dominates latency—has been left untouched.

To tackle this, the authors propose a framework that decouples VLM backbone depth ($V$), action expert depth ($A$), and denoising steps ($D$) into three independent, freely configurable compute axes. Lightweight Exit Transformers are attached at intermediate depths of a frozen VLA and trained via distillation. Furthermore, they introduce a KV Cache synthesis mechanism that smoothly fills in the missing keys and values required by deeper action expert layers when the VLM exits early.

Experimental results reveal clear complementary roles: reducing $V$ cuts total operations (FLOPs), reducing $A$ dramatically slashes latency, and adjusting $D$ improves both. The authors also demonstrate that optimal compute allocation is task-dependent: dexterity-heavy tasks demand a deeper expert, whereas visually challenging tasks require a deeper VLM.
contributions: Formulated backbone depth (V), action expert depth (A), and denoising steps (D) as three independently controllable axes, building an early-exit framework that can be retrofitted without retraining the original policy from scratch.
Introduced a KV Cache synthesis mechanism that allows deep action expert execution even after early VLM exits, enabling flexible cross-layer configurations with minimal computational overhead.
Validated the approach across two models (SmolVLA, π_0.5) and two benchmarks (LIBERO, Meta-World), reducing latency by 79.2% and FLOPs by 31.8% while improving mean success rate by 5.6%.
Experimentally proved that optimal compute allocation across the three axes differs significantly based on task characteristics (dexterity-heavy vs. visually demanding).

sections.heading: Why are robot VLAs so heavy? A new perspective across three compute axes
sections.summary: While flow-matching VLAs deliver impressive generalist control, their heavy inference computational cost hampers real-time robot execution. Looking beyond prior work, the authors focus on the overlooked depth of the action expert, proposing a 3-axis compute allocation framework alongside backbone depth and denoising steps.
sections.details:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are end-to-end policies that map camera observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception directly to continuous robot actions. Recently, flow-matching policies—which iteratively refine action trajectories from noise—have become mainstream for generating smoother and more precise motion.

Yet, computational cost remains a serious barrier. In flow matching, outputting a single action chunk requires multiple sequential denoising steps. While earlier work attempted to speed up VLAs, most efforts focused on cutting layers from the parameter-heavy VLM backbone (reducing FLOPs) or reducing denoising steps. Consequently, the depth of the action expert, which executes at every single denoising step and dominates runtime latency, remained fixed.

This is where this paper steps in. The authors treat VLM backbone depth ($V$), action expert depth ($A$), and denoising steps ($D$) as three decoupled compute axes that can be jointly controlled. Crucially, the VLM runs only once per action chunk, whereas the action expert repeats across every denoising step; thus, reducing each axis impacts latency and FLOPs in fundamentally different ways.

Moreover, the compute budget required varies by task. For instance, a stick-push task demands delicate contact control and thus requires action expert depth, while a box-close task requires spatial visual perception and depends on VLM depth. This study demonstrates that flexibly combining all three axes substantially pushes the Pareto frontier across inference speed, compute, and task success rate.

sections.heading: Blind spots in prior work: Why couldn't action experts be truncated before?
sections.summary: Techniques like layer pruning, caching, and early exits are common for VLA efficiency. However, existing work has focused solely on VLM reduction or fewer denoising steps, leaving action expert depth tightly bound and unaddressed as an independent axis.
sections.details:
Large models for robotics started with discrete action tokenization architectures like RT-2 and OpenVLA. However, due to precision limits in discretization, models evolved toward flow-matching architectures like $\pi_0$ that handle continuous multimodal trajectories. Efforts to slim down backbones have also advanced, as seen in SmolVLA and TinyVLA.

Early exits are a popular technique for accelerating inference, attaching heads to intermediate layers to stop computation once sufficient information is gathered. In the VLA realm, works such as DeeR-VLA have applied early exits to the VLM backbone. Other approaches include SnapFlow, which distills denoising into a single step, and A1, which halts computation based on consecutive prediction agreement.

However, existing methods like A1 couple the VLM backbone and action expert to exit at the exact same depth. The key novelty here is decoupling VLM depth $V$ and action expert depth $A$ into completely independent axes. Enabled by the newly introduced KV Cache synthesis mechanism, this framework can be easily applied to any existing flow-matching VLA via lightweight post-training distillation without modifying pretrained weights.

sections.heading: Mastering three compute axes: Exit Transformers and KV Cache synthesis
sections.summary: Lightweight Exit Transformers are placed at intermediate layers of a frozen VLA to distill final-layer representations. Additionally, a KV Cache synthesis mechanism uses minimal linear projections to fill in missing key-value representations when running a shallow VLM alongside a deeper expert.
sections.details:
### III-A Preliminaries and Architecture
A flow-matching VLA processes a prefix ($M$ tokens) encoding camera images and language prompts, alongside a suffix ($H$ tokens) containing robot state and noisy action candidates. The base model features a VLM backbone and an action expert sharing the same number of layers $N$. Each expert layer $i$ uses cross-attention over keys ($K$) and values ($V$) from the corresponding backbone layer $i-1$. At inference time, $D$ Euler integration steps are run to reconstruct the final action chunk from noise.

### III-B 3-Axis Compute Budget $(V, A, D)$
Under this framework, compute resources are configured using the tuple $(V, A, D)$:
- **VLM Exit Transformer ($V$)**: A lightweight single-block Transformer (ET) is attached at backbone depth $V$. It compensates for skipped layers and outputs a prefix representation $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_V$ close to the final layer.
- **Action Expert Exit Transformer ($A$)**: A similar single-block ET is attached at action expert depth $A$. Instead of latent representations, it directly predicts the velocity vector $v_\theta^{(A)}$ through the action head, skipping the remaining $(N - A)/N$ layers across all denoising steps.
- **Denoising Steps ($D$)**: The number of Euler integration steps. This requires zero additional parameters, allowing straightforward runtime trade-offs between accuracy and compute.

### III-C KV Cache Synthesis Mechanism
A major structural challenge emerges: if the VLM backbone exits at a shallow depth (e.g., $V=4$), deeper action expert layers (e.g., $A=8$) lack the corresponding backbone $K$ and $V$ representations to attend to.
To resolve this, the authors introduce KV Cache synthesis. The representation $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_V$ from the backbone ET is linearly projected using skipped layers' specific weight matrices ($\mathbf{W}_{k,i}$ and $\mathbf{W}_{v,i}$). Skipping attention and feed-forward networks entirely, it only evaluates normalization, two linear projections, and Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) all at once to populate the cache. This enables flexible $A > V$ configurations (action expert deeper than backbone) without adding computational overhead.

### III-D Training Formulation
During training, base VLA model weights remain frozen, and only the added ETs are trained via distillation. The VLM ET is trained using cosine distance to the final-layer representation and action velocity MSE, while the expert ET is trained on the flow-matching loss and final velocity MSE. This keeps the original policy intact, allowing instant rollback to full performance. Parameter overhead is minimal: SmolVLA (605M total) adds only 3.1M for expert ETs and 9.8M for VLM ETs, while $\pi_{0.5}$ (3.3B total) adds 23.6M and 110.1M respectively (an increase of just 2.1% to 4.1%).

sections.heading: Impressive Pareto improvements: Boosting success rates while cutting latency by ~80%
sections.summary: Evaluations on the LIBERO and Meta-World benchmarks show that the optimal joint configuration reduces latency by 79.2% and FLOPs by 31.8% compared to the full-compute base model, while raising mean success rate by 5.6%.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
The framework was evaluated on LIBERO (featuring long-horizon tasks) and Meta-World MT-50 (50 tasks across four difficulty levels). Experiments utilized SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ as base models, training ETs on checkpoints fine-tuned in the LeRobot framework. Metrics include task success rate (SR), computational FLOPs, and runtime latency measured at batch size 1.

### IV-B Single-Axis Trade-Offs and Joint Configurations (RQ1)
Varying each axis individually revealed clear divisions of labor:
- **VLM Depth ($V$)**: Most effective at slashing FLOPs, but since it runs only once per chunk, latency reduction is modest.
- **Expert Depth ($A$)**: Cuts through every single denoising iteration, dramatically reducing latency by nearly half.
- **Denoising Steps ($D$)**: A parameter-free lever reducing both latency and FLOPs; moderately reducing steps even boosted success rate in certain cases.

Combining these into an optimal joint configuration $(V, A, D)$ achieved an average 79.2% reduction in latency and a 31.8% reduction in FLOPs compared to the base model, while boosting average success rate by 5.6%.

### IV-C Task-Dependent Compute Requirements (RQ2)
Analyzing all 50 Meta-World tasks revealed that the full-compute model was optimal in only 11/50 tasks for SmolVLA and 22/50 tasks for $\pi_{0.5}$. Selecting task-optimal configurations elevated average success rate from 60.7% to 79.5% for SmolVLA, and from 64.9% to 75.9% for $\pi_{0.5}$.
Furthermore, requirements varied sharply by task nature. For example, the "hammer" task requires coarse visual cues, maintaining 100% success rate with VLM depth reduced to 4 layers, but collapses from 93% to 7% when the expert is truncated. Conversely, the "faucet-open" task relies on fine visual alignment; reducing the VLM plunges success rate from 100% to 0%, while expert truncation leaves the 100% success rate untouched.

### IV-D Ablation Studies (RQ3)
Compared to naive layer truncation without distillation, ET distillation boosted success rates by up to 86%, particularly at shallow depths. Additionally, removing KV Cache synthesis caused compute costs to surge, while the synthesis itself caused virtually zero degradation in success rate, validating the architecture's efficiency.

sections.heading: Conclusion and outlook: Turning robot compute from a fixed constraint into a control variable
sections.summary: This study presents a framework to independently govern backbone depth, expert depth, and denoising steps in flow-matching VLAs. It demonstrates that computational resources in robotics should not be viewed as static constraints, but rather as dynamic control variables tailored to the task.
sections.details:
This paper introduced an early-exit framework that independently configures VLM depth $V$, action expert depth $A$, and denoising steps $D$ to slash inference overhead in flow-matching VLAs.

By adding lightweight Exit Transformers and an efficient KV Cache synthesis mechanism to frozen models, the approach significantly improves trade-offs between inference speed and task success rate. Most intriguingly, the computational bottlenecks depend heavily on the task at hand. Allocating compute to the expert for high-dexterity tasks and to the VLM for complex perceptual tasks proves to be a powerful strategy.

For future work, the authors highlight developing algorithms that autonomously and adaptively select the optimal $(V, A, D)$ combination online, adjusting to task difficulty and per-timestep demands rather than relying on grid search.

takeaways: In accelerating VLAs, cutting action expert depth—which executes at every step of the denoising loop—is the true key to reducing latency, while the VLM backbone primarily governs FLOPs.
Reducing denoising steps (D) not only accelerates inference without extra parameters, but can also improve task success rate by avoiding excessive noise accumulation.
There is a distinct compute trade-off: high-dexterity tasks mandate action expert depth, whereas visual recognition and spatial localization tasks require VLM depth.
KV Cache synthesis enables asymmetric configurations where the VLM stays shallow while the action expert runs deep, maximizing compute efficiency.
limitations: The placement of intermediate early-exit layers (where ETs are attached) must be predetermined manually, leaving the optimal layer selection across different architectures an open question.
Selecting the optimal compute budget (V, A, D) per task currently relies on empirical search, and a mechanism for fully autonomous, online adaptive selection at inference time has yet to be built.
Experiments are restricted to simulated environments (LIBERO, Meta-World), leaving the real-world impact of sensor noise and inference latency on closed-loop hardware control unverified.
